description: This walk takes you to Northey Island on the Blackwater Estuary in Essex. The National Trust owned island is located near Maldon and is a fine place for birdwatching in the Blackwater Estuary. Walk Report October 12th 2026 By Martin Ellis: We parked at Promenade Park in Maldon (postcode CM9 5UR for your satnavs) and set off towards Northey Island, looking forward to exploring somewhere a little different from the usual countryside walk. The route begins by the park's boating lake before joining the England Coast Path along the sea wall. It was a breezy day, with wide skies over the Blackwater Estuary and plenty of birds moving across the mudflats. I liked the feeling of being close to the water so soon after leaving the town behind, and the views opened up as we approached the island.The walk across the causeway was one of the highlights. Northey is a genuinely unusual place, connected to the mainland by a narrow crossing that disappears beneath the tide. Looking across the estuary, with the saltmarsh stretching away on either side, it felt surprisingly remote for somewhere so close to Maldon. There are extensive views over the water, and we stopped several times to watch the birds feeding along the shoreline. It is worth remembering that the causeway is covered for roughly three hours either side of high tide, so checking the Maldon tide times before setting off is essential. Never attempt the crossing if water covers it, and allow plenty of time to return safely.Northey Island is famous for its connection with the Battle of Maldon in AD 991, when Anglo-Saxon forces fought Viking raiders. The battle is commemorated in one of the best-known surviving Old English poems, which adds an intriguing historical dimension to this otherwise peaceful landscape. As we crossed the causeway, I tried to imagine how different the estuary must have looked more than a thousand years ago. Today, the island is much quieter, with farmland, sea walls and wildlife taking centre stage.Once on the island, we followed the marked route through the fields and along the tracks, keeping an eye out for the pink waymarkers. The walk is mostly flat, although some of the grass paths are uneven and could be slippery after rain. One of our first stops was the bird hide, overlooking a freshwater pond created as part of the conservation work here. Water voles have been introduced to the pond, while the surrounding fields provide important feeding and roosting areas for birds. In winter, Brent geese gather in impressive numbers around the estuary, and waders such as redshank, curlew and plovers can be seen on the mudflats.The scenery changes as the trail follows the sea wall and passes areas where the landscape is gradually returning to saltmarsh. The National Trust has been allowing the tide to reach selected fields to create new wetland habitat, helping the island adapt to rising sea levels. I found this an interesting aspect of the walk, because the landscape isn't simply being preserved as it is; it is being allowed to change in a way that benefits wildlife. Across the marshes, we could see Osea Island, with its distinctive towered house standing out in the distance.We continued along the tracks between hedges, eventually reaching a bench with lovely views across the estuary towards Heybridge Basin and Maldon. It was a good place to pause, have a drink and watch the birds working along the mudflats. Other walkers have described the island as a peaceful escape from crowds, and I could understand that appeal. There isn't a succession of major attractions here, and some stretches are enclosed by hedges, but the open views, solitude and sense of being surrounded by the estuary make it worthwhile if you enjoy quiet, nature-focused walks.The return journey took us back along the track to the causeway and then along the sea wall towards Promenade Park. By this point, the tide and the changing patterns of water across the mudflats had given the scenery a different appearance. We finished back at the park, where toilets and refreshments are available, which is useful as there are no visitor facilities on the island itself. The statue of Byrhtnoth at the far end of the promenade is also worth seeing if you have time, with its connection to the Battle of Maldon and views back across the estuary.At just over three miles, this is a manageable circular walk, although I would allow around two hours to enjoy it without rushing. The most important part of planning is the tide: check the local times carefully before leaving, and don't cross the causeway if it is covered. Keep dogs on leads or under close control, particularly during the ground-nesting bird season, and stay on the permitted paths rather than venturing onto the mudflats or saltmarsh. Northey Island won't suit everyone, especially if you're looking for a route packed with landmarks, but for a peaceful estuary walk with wildlife, wide skies and a fascinating piece of English history, I thought it was well worth the visit.
